Twelve passages from the Epic of Gilgamesh

Written on clay tablets more than four thousand years ago, the epic tells how an invincible king discovers death through the loss of a friend. These are the twelve episodes that hold the work together, each with a passage from the poem. Each corresponds to a room of the three-dimensional journey.

Tablet mode: the signs show proper names, numerals and the opening words of the poem in their original script, Akkadian cuneiform (Noto Sans Cuneiform typeface, OFL licence). They are not a translation of the texts.

𒁹 𒀭𒄑 𒌷𒀕ᵈGIŠ · URU.UNUG — Gilgamesh · Uruk

Station I · Courtyard of UrukThe Tyrant King of Uruk

Gilgamesh, two-thirds god and one-third man, rules Uruk with perfect strength but boundless arrogance. The nobles complain to the gods, for the king leaves no son to his father and no maiden to her mother, abusing his power day and night.

Gilgamesh leaves no son to his father, no maiden to the warrior, no wife to her husband.

Epic of Gilgamesh · our rendering based on Muss-Arnolt (1901) and Jastrow and Clay (1920), public domain

𒈫 𒀭𒀀𒊒𒊒 𒀭𒂗𒆠𒆕ᵈa-ru-ru · ᵈen-ki-dù — Aruru · Enkidu

Station II · Chamber of EnkiduThe Creation of Enkidu

Heeding the complaints, the goddess Aruru fashions Enkidu from clay, a wild being meant to be Gilgamesh’s rival. Enkidu lives on the steppe, his body covered in hair; he lives at peace among the beasts and protects them from hunters.

Aruru washed her hands, pinched off a little clay and cast it on the ground: so she created Enkidu.

Epic of Gilgamesh · our rendering based on Muss-Arnolt (1901) and Jastrow and Clay (1920), public domain

𒐈 𒀭𒂗𒆠𒆕ᵈen-ki-dù — Enkidu

Station III · Chamber of EnkiduThe Humanisation of Enkidu

To civilise Enkidu, Gilgamesh sends a hierodule, a sacred prostitute. After six days and seven nights of human love, Enkidu finds that the animals flee from him; his bodily strength wanes, but his mind grows “wise” and he comes to understand the world.

You are sublime, Enkidu; you shall be like a god.

Epic of Gilgamesh · our rendering based on Muss-Arnolt (1901) and Jastrow and Clay (1920), public domain

𒐉 𒀭𒄑 𒀭𒂗𒆠𒆕ᵈGIŠ · ᵈen-ki-dù — Gilgamesh · Enkidu

Station IV · Courtyard of the AssemblyThe Meeting and the Heroic Friendship

Enkidu arrives in Uruk to challenge the king’s tyranny. The two fight fiercely before the House of the Assembly “like two wild bulls”, but once they recognise each other as equals the struggle ends, and they seal an unbreakable friendship that will bind them for ever.

Gilgamesh set his foot upon the ground: his anger abated, his breast grew calm.

Epic of Gilgamesh · our rendering based on Muss-Arnolt (1901) and Jastrow and Clay (1920), public domain

𒐊 𒀭𒌓ᵈUTU — Shamash, the Sun

Station V · Cedar ForestThe Expedition to the Cedar Forest

Seeking eternal glory and to “win a name”, Gilgamesh resolves to travel to the Cedar Forest and defeat Humbaba, the monstrous guardian appointed by the gods. Despite Enkidu’s fear, Gilgamesh insists that only the gods are immortal and that a man must fight for his fame.

If I fall, I shall have established my name.

Epic of Gilgamesh · our rendering based on Muss-Arnolt (1901) and Jastrow and Clay (1920), public domain

𒐋 𒄷𒉿𒉿ḫu-wa-wa — Huwawa (Humbaba)

Station VI · Lair of HumbabaThe Defeat of Humbaba

Helped by the eight winds sent by the god Shamash, the heroes pin Humbaba down. Though the giant begs for mercy, the friends kill him and cut off his head, destroying the guardian of the sacred forest.

His roar is a flood, his mouth is fire, his breath is death.

Epic of Gilgamesh · our rendering based on Muss-Arnolt (1901) and Jastrow and Clay (1920), public domain

𒐌 𒀭𒈹ᵈINANNA — Ishtar

Station VII · Square of the BullThe Rejection of Ishtar and the Bull of Heaven

The goddess Ishtar falls in love with Gilgamesh, but he rejects her with insults, reminding her of the fate of her former lovers. Enraged, Ishtar sends the Bull of Heaven to destroy Uruk, but the two friends kill it and humiliate the goddess.

Enkidu attacked the Bull of Heaven and seized it by its thick tail.

Epic of Gilgamesh · our rendering based on Muss-Arnolt (1901) and Jastrow and Clay (1920), public domain

𒐍 𒀭𒂗𒆠𒆕ᵈen-ki-dù — Enkidu

Station VIII · Chamber of Enkidu, emptyThe Death of Enkidu

The gods decide that Enkidu must die as punishment for the friends’ deeds. Enkidu falls ill and has terrifying visions of the world of the dead. After his death, Gilgamesh sinks into utter grief, mourning his friend like a hired mourner and refusing to accept his loss.

Gilgamesh wept bitterly for his friend, and lay stretched upon the ground.

Epic of Gilgamesh · our rendering based on Muss-Arnolt (1901) and Jastrow and Clay (1920), public domain

𒐎 𒆳𒈠𒋗KUR ma-šu — Mount Mashu

Station IX · Mountains of MashuThe Journey through the Mountains of Mashu

Terrified of his own death, Gilgamesh sets out to find Ut-napishtim and gain eternal life. On his way he must cross the mountains of Mashu, where he meets the fearsome scorpion-men, guardians of the gates of the Sun.

Scorpion-men guard its gate: their terror is so deep that to look on them is death.

Epic of Gilgamesh · our rendering based on Muss-Arnolt (1901) and Jastrow and Clay (1920), public domain

𒌋 𒌓𒍣UD.ZI — Uta-napishti

Station X · Island of Ut-napishtimThe Meeting with Ut-napishtim and the Flood

Gilgamesh crosses the “Waters of Death” and finds Ut-napishtim, who reveals that immortality was a unique gift granted after he survived the Great Flood, and explains that the gods decide life and death without revealing the final day.

I looked about in every direction, and behold: all was sea.

Epic of Gilgamesh · our rendering based on Muss-Arnolt (1901) and Jastrow and Clay (1920), public domain

𒌋𒁹 𒀭𒄑ᵈGIŠ — Gilgamesh

Station XI · Ascent to the wallsThe Plant of Youth and the Final Failure

Ut-napishtim reveals where to find a plant that restores youth. Gilgamesh brings it up from the bottom of the sea, but while he bathes, a serpent steals it. The hero finally understands that his only lasting legacy will be the walls of Uruk that he himself built.

A serpent rose swiftly; the plant slipped from his hands.

Epic of Gilgamesh · our rendering based on Muss-Arnolt (1901) and Jastrow and Clay (1920), public domain

𒌋𒈫 𒌷𒀕URU.UNUG — Uruk

Station XII · Top of the wallsWhat Remains: the Walls of Uruk

Back in Uruk, without the plant and without his friend, Gilgamesh climbs with Urshanabi the ferryman to the top of the walls he had built. He asks him to examine the foundations, the baked brick, the seven layers of bitumen: the work still stands. He did not win eternal life, but he discovers another kind of permanence: the kind a well-built city leaves behind. The king who began by abusing his strength ends by understanding what power is truly for.

Examine its foundation, inspect its brickwork: see if its wall is not of baked brick.

Epic of Gilgamesh · our rendering based on Muss-Arnolt (1901) and Jastrow and Clay (1920), public domain

Testimonies

Real artefacts placed along the journey, between one station and the next. They do not illustrate the story: they bear witness to it.

Transparency

This experience was conceived, researched and directed by its author. Artificial intelligence tools were used as creative and technical support during design, programming, translation and production. The selection, organisation, review and editorial direction of the content are the author’s.

The station images were generated with artificial intelligence, and this is stated next to each one. The architecture, textures and sound of the journey are generated by code in the browser itself.

Quotations are our own rendering based on the public-domain English versions by W. Muss-Arnolt (1901) and M. Jastrow and A. T. Clay (1920). Cuneiform signs use the Noto Sans Cuneiform typeface (SIL Open Font License).

This page uses no cookies, loads no third-party resources and records no data about its visitors.
